subcategory: evergreen New Zealand coastal shade shrub

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; houpara tolerates coastal wind and salt spray but is only reliably hardy where winter lows stay above the mid-teens Fahrenheit.

directions: Houpara is a dense, rounded New Zealand shrub valued for its thick, glossy, palmate leaves divided into three to five broad, leathery leaflets with shallow serrations near the tip, giving it a tropical look despite its tough constitution. Clusters of small, inconspicuous greenish flowers appear on older wood and are followed by dark purple-black fruit on female plants when a male grows nearby. It handles everything from full coastal sun to partial woodland shade, making it a flexible filler or background shrub where a bold tropical texture is wanted without tropical fuss. Prune lightly after flowering to keep a dense habit, and give it sharp drainage since wet winter feet are its main vulnerability.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

subcategory: variegated evergreen New Zealand shade shrub

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained soil in partial shade; the golden variegation is brightest with some protection from the hottest afternoon sun.

directions: 'Gold Splash' is a compact sport of the New Zealand shrub houpara, selected for its leathery leaflets irregularly splashed and margined in bright golden yellow over a dark green base, lighting up a shaded corner far more than the plain species. It stays noticeably smaller and denser than straight Pseudopanax lessonii, making it useful in containers, mixed borders, or as a specimen where year-round color is wanted without flowers. Give it reliable drainage and a sheltered site, since both hard frost and scorching midday sun can damage the variegated foliage. Light trimming after new growth hardens off keeps the rounded shape tidy.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in very well-drained soil in dappled sun to bright shade; growth is slow and even slower in deeper shade, so give young plants a spot with at least some direct or filtered light.

directions: The toothed lancewood is an even stranger relative of the better-known horoeka, spending decades as a single rigid, unbranched stem clothed in narrow, stiffly leathery juvenile leaves edged with widely spaced, forward-pointing teeth, like a row of small fangs along each margin. This odd juvenile phase is thought to have evolved as a deterrent to browsing by extinct giant moa, and it persists far longer than in most other New Zealand lancewoods before the plant finally branches into a softer-leaved adult crown. Grow it in part sun to bright shade in sharply drained soil, and expect a slow, architectural accent rather than a quick screening plant. It makes an unusual specimen in a gravel garden or large container where its sculptural outline can be appreciated up close.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring in sheltered, free-draining soil; puka tolerates full coastal sun but develops its largest, glossiest leaves in partial to full shade, and is somewhat less cold-hardy than its relative Griselinia littoralis.

directions: In the wild this New Zealand native often begins life as an epiphyte lodged in the forks of forest trees before sending roots down to the ground, but in cultivation it grows readily as a free-standing shrub or small multi-stemmed tree. Its broad, intensely glossy, fresh-green leaves are noticeably larger and shinier than those of the more common Griselinia littoralis, especially on plants grown in shade rather than open sun. Small greenish flowers are followed by orange-red fruit on female plants when a male grows nearby. Site it out of the harshest wind and winter cold, since it is a touch more tender than its coastal cousin, and let it develop an open, informal shape rather than clipping it hard.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, sheltered from drying wind; mamaku is frost-tender and the black trunk itself needs regular moisture, so it is best grown in a humid, protected courtyard or large container outside the mildest zones.

directions: Mamaku is one of the fastest-growing and largest of the Southern Hemisphere tree ferns, recognizable by its slender, strikingly black, rough-textured trunk that can add well over a foot of height a year under good conditions, eventually supporting a broad crown of long, arching, deep-green fronds. Unlike more sun-tolerant tree ferns, it performs best with filtered or partial shade and shelter from wind, since exposed fronds scorch and tatter easily. Keep the trunk and soil consistently moist through the growing season, since mamaku draws much of its water through the fibrous trunk surface rather than roots alone. In marginal zones grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover for winter, or wrap the trunk ahead of hard frost.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, acidic, humus-poor but mineral-rich soil with morning sun and afternoon shade; ponga is New Zealand's national emblem fern and grows slowly, resenting both full sun and deep, dry shade.

directions: The silver fern is New Zealand's most iconic tree fern, named for the brilliant white-silver undersides of its fronds that have made it a national symbol, instantly distinguishing it from the plain green reverse of most other tree ferns. It grows considerably slower than Cyathea medullaris or cooperi, building a stout trunk over many years while staying more compact and tolerant of cooler, drier air than most tree ferns, though it still wants shelter from drying wind. Give it bright, filtered light rather than full sun, which scorches the fronds, and lean, leached, humus-poor soil rather than rich garden loam, mimicking the native forest-floor conditions where it is adapted to recycle minerals rather than organic matter. Mature fronds held up to the light show the silver reverse to best effect, so site it where the undersides can be glimpsed from a path below.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs or rooted cuttings in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; wire-netting bush is drought tolerant once established and needs little supplemental water beyond its first season.

directions: Wire-netting bush earns its name from its tangled, interlacing, nearly zig-zagging branches, a growth habit called divarication that is common among New Zealand shrubs and thought to have evolved as a defense against browsing moa. Small, dark, grayish leaves cling close to the wiry stems, in late spring giving way to a scattering of small bright-yellow, star-shaped flowers that are followed by attractive orange-red berries in summer. Its tight, twiggy outline makes it a distinctive textural accent or low informal hedge in a part-shade border, especially effective where winter sun lights up the bare branch structure. It is tough and undemanding once rooted in, tolerating poor soil, wind, and drought with little care.

planting.note: Plant the bulb with its neck at the soil surface in humus-rich, free-draining soil in bright shade; this is one of the most genuinely shade-adapted Haemanthus species and will scorch badly in any direct sun.

directions: Unlike its larger, more sun-tolerant relatives, this diminutive South African bulb grows naturally flat against the forest floor beneath dense evergreen canopy, where its broad, softly velvety, silver-green leaves lie almost prostrate on the leaf litter. In autumn it sends up short, dense, brush-like heads of small white flowers tipped with pale stamens, held just above the foliage rather than on a tall stalk. It stays evergreen in frost-free, humid conditions rather than going fully dormant like many of its relatives, so keep it lightly moist year-round rather than drying it out completely. Its small scale and genuine deep-shade tolerance make it a choice collector's bulb for a shaded terrarium, pot, or woodland container rather than an open garden bed.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall with the top third exposed in humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to part shade; this cultivar is nearly evergreen in frost-free, humid gardens but benefits from a brief drier rest in late summer as old leaves decline.

directions: 'Lemon Flame' is a selected form of the South African forest lily grown as much for its foliage as its flowers, with broad, glossy strap leaves showing irregular creamy-yellow variegation along the margins and midribs. In late winter it sends up the same sturdy, mottled flower stalk as the species, but topped with a dense raceme of pale greenish-yellow, tubular flowers rather than the usual pink to coral shades, giving a softer color effect in a shaded bed or container. Like the species it is a true shade-to-part-shade forest bulb from the Eastern Cape, thriving under canopy where moisture is reasonably steady through winter and spring. Grow it in a pot where it can be given a sheltered, shaded spot and brought under cover if winter temperatures threaten to drop below the high 20s Fahrenheit.

common_name: Copper New Zealand Iris (Orange NZ Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown clumps in spring in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; foliage color is most intense with more light, but the plant adapts readily to light to moderate shade as well.

directions: This creeping New Zealand perennial spreads by rhizomes into loose colonies of stiff, narrow, iris-like fans, with foliage that flushes copper, bronze, and burnt-orange, deepening in color in brighter or harsher conditions and staying more olive-green in deeper shade. Small white, three-petaled flowers appear in spring to early summer just above the foliage, followed by decorative seed capsules that split to reveal orange seeds valued in dried arrangements. Its running habit makes it useful as a slowly spreading groundcover or edging plant at the sunnier fringe of a woodland bed, where its warm foliage tones contrast nicely against green ferns and hostas. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to control spread and keep color vigorous.
